items.headline: OpenAI and Broadcom unveil Jalapeno, OpenAI's first custom inference accelerator
items.diff_narrative: A net-new top lead with no June 24 antecedent; yesterday's slate opened with the Sakana Fugu independent reality check, which drops off this run as no fresh state-change has surfaced on it. Today's catalyst is OpenAI and Broadcom unveiling Jalapeno on June 24, the first chip from a multi-year co-design effort and what OpenAI frames as its first "Intelligence Processor" — an accelerator architected around OpenAI's view of LLM inference rather than training. The fresh artifact carries concrete claims: engineering samples are already running machine-learning workloads in the lab at production target frequency and power, OpenAI says early testing shows performance per watt "substantially better than current state-of-the-art," and the companies describe Jalapeno as the first step in a multi-generation compute platform with initial data-center deployment targeted by the end of 2026 at gigawatt scale. Broadcom's Tomahawk fabric (rated up to 1.6 terabits per second) wires the accelerators together and Celestia is collaborating on the custom server-rack design, marking this as a full rack-scale inference platform. The structural read is that the largest frontier-model buyer is now following the hyperscaler playbook of designing its own inference ASIC to escape merchant-GPU economics, placing a named OpenAI-Broadcom part alongside the Google-Broadcom TPU and Amazon Trainium lineage. Final performance numbers are still being measured and a fuller technical report is promised in coming months, so the per-watt advantage remains a vendor claim, not yet independently benchmarked.

items.headline: Gartner puts a number on agentic-coding economics: AI coding spend projected to overtake the average developer's salary by 2028
items.diff_narrative: A fresh analyst/economics lead with no June 24 counterpart, replacing yesterday's Micron-Anthropic Series H HBM thread, which carries no new evidence today. Gartner published a research note on June 24 predicting that by 2028 the cost of AI coding will surpass the average developer's salary, driven by rising LLM token consumption and the shift to consumption-based pricing for agentic coding tools. The new, quotable thresholds are the news: Gartner Peer Insights data cited in the note shows 23 percent of technology leaders already spend between $200 and $500 per developer per month on tokens, and 6 percent of organizations pay more than $2,000 per developer per month, with the firm warning that the steepest cost escalation comes from ungoverned autonomy in agent-driven workflows, bloated context windows, and the absence of structured feedback to optimize usage. The analysis ties directly to the autonomous-developer-loop tools (the Cursor / Claude Code / Codex CLI class of agentic IDEs) whose per-seat token bills are the cost center, reframing the productivity narrative as a governance problem: Gartner's explicit position is that token discipline will not arise spontaneously and that organizations need a governed engineering operating model before scaled agent deployment outruns the gains. This is a forward forecast from an analyst house rather than a shipped product, so the 2028 crossover is a projection, not an observed event, but it is a net-new named numeric position on the unit economics of the agent-harness category.

items.headline: Bay Area / SV AI events calendar rolls forward; Automate, AI Tinkerers Demo Night, and Snowflake Dev Day reach end and drop off
items.diff_narrative: The forward-looking three-track events bullet carries over from June 24 with the calendar advanced. The headline change is that the events that closed at the start of this week now reach their end and drop off the forward list: Automate 2026 (June 22-25, McCormick Place), the AI Tinkerers SF Offensive Security Demo Night, and Snowflake's virtual Dev Day (both June 25). With Automate aged out of the AI-chip/hardware slot, the mainstream dev/data track moves to the AI Engineer World's Fair taking over Moscone West, with the official AIE World's Fair Hackathon run with Cerebral Valley June 27-28, an optional New Engineer Orientation June 28, and main programming June 29 through July 2. Further out the calendar holds unchanged: GitHub Universe (October 28-29) and AWS re:Invent (November 30-December 4) on the mainstream track; Black Hat USA's AI Summit (August 1-6), SecurityWeek's AI Risk Summit (August 11-12), OWASP Global AppSec USA (November 5-6), and Zenity's AI Agent Security Summit series on the security track; AMD's Advancing AI 2026 (July 22-23, Instinct MI400-series focus, keynote July 23), Hot Chips 2026 (August 23-25, Stanford), and the AI Infra Summit (September 15-17, Santa Clara) on the chip/hardware track. All three sub-tracks remain covered.
